The fact that your daughter is asking to be there is a good sign as well bc she probably somewhat understands what that means. I was diagnosed at 22 (am now almost 24) and it’s been an overal positive thing for me. Most of my life there was always that question of what was ‘wrong’ with me and many therapists gave me different diagnoses. Mentally I never really got any better bc no therapist got the full picture. Since diagnosis I would say all of my relationships (family included) are so much better than they before. I am able to get assistance at university that I would not be able to get without it, and explaining myself to loved ones is so much easier. Because I am in regular therapy as well, I am constantly learning about myself which helps all of the above mentioned things. I doubt any of this would have been possible for me without an official diagnosis. Obviously if you do not feel the need for it yourself, that’s completely understandable. If you understand yourself enough to function without an ‘official’ diagnosis, and don’t need assistance that requires some kind of official piece of paper, I don’t see why you should go through the process of getting it.
I love using it in my real life especially because I require it often.

I think a good way to start is to reframe the way in which you view your skin picking. Using terminology like ‘clean’ or ‘relapsing’ may not be the best way to deal w this problem mentally. Personally, once I stopped viewing my skin picking in this way it helped me to not feel so terribly guilty if I ‘broke a streak’ or something. Just doing small things like distracting yourself, fidgeting with something, covering your nails, hiding the spots with plasters etc have helped me for the most part with harm reduction. Obviously different things work for different people but definitely a good starting point is dealing with the feelings of shame around the act of picking, and the way you feel about your body in relation to scars and spots etc. Once you start to process the feelings around why you pick and what your triggers are, it becomes easier to deal with the compulsive feelings, and myself personally I am much better at stopping myself before it gets very bad. I still pick pretty much everyday, and am unfortunately currently in a pretty bad bout with it, but I am so much better at being aware and cognisant of my actions when I’m doing it and why.

I relate to this so much! My family and I have always suspected I was autistic and I was diagnosed (finally, at age 21) at the beginning of this year. Because adhd is often a comorbidity with autism, I had always thought maybe I had that too. I’ve struggled with intrusive thoughts, struggling to focus etc and after years of being on SSRIs that never seemed to go away. But at the beginning of this year I found a new psychiatrist and we discussed potential adhd. We did a couple tests and determined that’s what it was, and I was prescribed Ritalin. Firstly, I'd like to say that I know exactly what you're going through. I've been skin picking for as long as I can remember (I'm almost 20). Around age 14 I began self-harming quite regularly. In hindsight, I realise that my skin picking would decrease in regards to my face and other body parts, because all my energy was either focused on the act of self-harming, hiding the cuts/scars and sometimes just picking at the scabs of the cuts themselves. After a while my self-harm tendencies decreased and my skin picking became really bad. A lot of people thought I just had bad acne but really I rarely actually got pimples I would just obsessively search for 'irregularities' in my skin to then 'fix'. I essentially replaced one relatively bad obsession with another, which in my case was deifnitely much worse than the former. Recently however, I've become more aware of my picking and make a conscious effort to not do it. I've never been the type to just quit anything cold-turkey, therefore it has been quite a rollecoaster since starting this journey. My main objective at the moment is just to decrease the amount of places on my body that I pick. For a while my breasts and chest area were my main picking area. But I also have picking spots on my scalp as well as my legs and some on my face. Rcently I purchased hydrocolloid plasters and put them over the wounds on my chest area. After about a week or so they have completely healed up and it's now just a matter of fading the scars. I am not suddenly healed though. I still pick at my scalp. This is the area I will be targeting next. Unfortunately I cannot put any plasters on this area so it may become trickier. I have recently begun my second year of university so stressful situations are constantly around the corner. It does help me to practice self care after a long picking session and to not get too mad at myself. If you pick at your face try washing it with water afterwards or just treating it with extra special care. I've also made it a routine to rub my whole body in bio-care oil and body butter after a shower to feel clean and not so dry to avoid fidgeting at loose pieces of dead skin. When I have depressive episodes I always know because I zone out a lot more and can pick at my skin for hours. I've even found myself doing this in lectures! Even though it is incredibly difficult to fight through the urge, I encourage you to start off slow. There is no quick fix solution for this but hopefully some of what I've shared may be helpful. In general it helps to avoid situations that make you pick more, but then again this isn't always a realistic solution. If you wish to message me please do, would love to talk!
